title: Ratio of the molar volume of pure B as a vapour to its molar volume as a liquid in an ideal solution
summary: Type the stem's data into a dark neon bench, press run, and watch it count 1000 g of A into a sealed container mole by mole, drop B in by molality and build the mole fraction from the dots, boil the solution until the gauge reaches the measured total and solve Raoult's law live for the vapour pressure of pure B, then fill two chambers with one mole of B each - a tiny liquid cube beside a vapour cube drawn at the honest edge ratio - before spraying the ratio across the screen.
subject: Chemistry
topic: Raoult's law for ideal solutions of two volatile liquids
subtopics: Molality to mole fraction, and why the solvent's molar mass is needed
Raoult's law for a binary ideal solution
Vapour pressure of a pure component recovered from a measured total
Molar volume of a liquid from its density
Molar volume of an ideal gas at a stated pressure
Converting mm Hg to atm to match the units of R
Dimensionless ratios of two molar quantities
concepts: Molality counts moles of solute per kilogram of solvent while mole fraction counts them against every mole present, so a molality always has to be converted before Raoult's law can be used - and the conversion is what the molar mass of A is given for
The mass of solvent taken is a free choice: x(B) = m / (m + 1000/M(A)) contains no w(A), so the answer is the same for 500 g or 2500 g of A
For an ideal solution each component's partial pressure is its pure vapour pressure times its own mole fraction, and the total is a straight line between p(A) and p(B)
With p(total), p(A) and both mole fractions known, Raoult's law has exactly one unknown left, which is what makes the first half of this question a one-line solve
A liquid's molar volume comes from density alone - M/rho - with no temperature and no pressure in it, because its molecules are already touching

Molar volume of pure B in the vapour phase means one mole of B alone at its own vapour pressure p(B), not at the mixture's total pressure and not at 1 atm - this is the single decision the whole question turns on
R quoted in L atm K-1 mol-1 forces the pressure into atmospheres, which is why the stem also hands over 1 atm = 760 mm Hg
Both molar volumes are per mole, so the ratio is a pure number: RTrho x 1000 / (M x p)
A vapour near a tenth of an atmosphere occupies about a thousand times the volume of the same mole of liquid, but in each linear direction the expansion is only the cube root of that - about 12.6
formulas: p(total) = p(A)deg x(A) + p(B)deg x(B)   (Raoult, ideal solution)
V(vapour, molar) = RT/p,  p(atm) = p(mm Hg)/760
ratio = R T rho(B) x 1000 / [M(B) x p(B)deg]  - dimensionless

derivedQuantities.closed_form: ratio = R T rho x 1000 / (M_B x p_B_pure)

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: the molality-to-mole-fraction conversion, the Raoult solve for p(B)deg, both molar volumes and the final division were each fixed independently

The choice of basis proved irrelevant rather than assumed: repeating the calculation on 500 g, 1000 g, 2500 g and 137 g of A returns x(B) = 0.2 in every case, matching the closed form m/(m + 1000/M(A)) computed in exact rational arithmetic - and the simulation reproduces this live, so sweeping the mass of A changes n(A) and n(B) on the gauges while the answer never moves

Raoult back-substitution: putting p(B)deg = 80 mm Hg back in gives 105(0.8) + 80(0.2) = 84 + 16 = 100 mm Hg, exactly the total the question states, and the direction is consistent because p(total) < p(A)deg requires p(B)deg < p(A)deg

The ratio computed twice by different routes: RT/p divided by M/rho gives 2000, and the closed form R T rho x 1000 / (M x p) gives 2000 to machine precision. V(vapour) itself was obtained both as RT/(p/760) and as RT x 760/p, both 228 L/mol

Scaling laws checked away from the paper's numbers: doubling T doubles the ratio, doubling p(B)deg halves it, doubling the density of the liquid doubles it and doubling M(B) halves it - exactly as RTrho/(Mp) requires, so the model is valid across its whole input range rather than at one point

Dimensions and magnitude: L mol-1 over L mol-1 leaves a pure number. At 1 atm and 300 K the molar volume would be 24 L mol-1, and at 80/760 atm it is 9.5 times larger, giving 228 - and a vapour near a tenth of an atmosphere occupying about 10^3 times a liquid's volume is the expected order of magnitude

The distractors reproduced deliberately, each as a run on the student's own data: using p(total) gives 1600, using p(A)deg gives 1523.81, forgetting the mm Hg to atm conversion gives 2.63, leaving the liquid volume in mL gives 2, reading 5 molal as x(B) = 5/20 gives 1882.35 and inverting the ratio gives 5 x 10-4. None is 2000
The impossible case handled rather than ignored: a total pressure at or below p(A)deg x(A) would need a negative vapour pressure for B, and the bench refuses to run, stating A's own contribution
Independent numeric script in exact fractions (verify15.py): 32 of 32 checks pass and the answer is 2000 with no floating-point rounding anywhere

Headless-browser run of the finished page: 111 assertions driving the whole flow - the chemistry the page is built on, the model's behaviour away from the question's numbers, the empty rail with the answer and p(B)deg nowhere on it, the refusal of a total pressure below A's own contribution, rejection of unreadable input, each of the four screens in turn with its equations written in the student's own numbers, pause and resume genuinely freezing and restarting the clock, the two cubes drawn at an edge ratio measured from the SVG and matching the cube root of the answer, a sixteen-frame leak sweep confirming the answer appears on no screen before the reveal, the suspense card, the graffiti reveal with its spray filter and particle burst, the header blinking once and stopping, the record and trial log, a second run at 450 K producing 3000 and a third at 2500 g of A producing 2000 again, all six traps, all three diagram views, the composition explorer, replay, speed, sound, theme toggle, a deck that fits in one window at 595 px, unique ids, accessible labels, a clean console and zero horizontal overflow at 390 px and 360 px
A separate reduced-motion run confirmed the blink and card animations are suppressed while the content and the answer remain complete

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which follows the same route and reports the same intermediate values (x(B) = 0.2, p(B)deg = 80 mm Hg, 228 L/mol and 0.114 L/mol) and the same answer, 2000. IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable at the time of writing
verification.note: Q.15 and Q.16 share one question stem in Section 4 of the paper. This simulation answers Q.15 only; the vapour-phase composition that Q.16 asks for is deliberately left out of the page so that question stays fresh. Section 4 is marked +2 for the correct value and 0 otherwise, unlike the +4/0 of Section 3.

interactivity: Enter the data, run the experiment, watch it produce the answer: an instrument rail you fill in, four screens you watch, and a ratio read off the finished run - about thirty seconds end to end

The experiment happens inside a dark neon chamber that stays dark in either page theme, with glass, depth and glow, while the page around it follows the light or dark theme like every other simulation in the library

Eight inputs, one for every quantity the stem gives - mass of A, molality, vapour pressure of pure A, measured total pressure, temperature, both molar masses and the density of liquid B - each with a typed box, a slider and a pair of large steppers, and each accepting 1/2, 5e-1 and similar forms
R and 1 atm = 760 mm Hg are shown as fixed givens rather than as inputs, because the question fixes them
Nine live instruments that stay blank until the run establishes them, so the rail shows exactly how much is known at any moment - and the ratio gauge stays blank until the very end
Nothing is precomputed: the bench runs on whatever is entered, reaches a different answer for different data, and refuses data it cannot reconcile
The bench refuses a total pressure at or below what A alone contributes and says why, quoting A's own partial pressure - the one physically impossible region of the input space
Screen 1 weighs A into a sealed vessel and draws one dot per mole, so n(A) = w(A)/M(A) is counted rather than asserted, with a note saying what one dot is worth when the numbers get large

Screen 2 drops B in at the entered molality and then builds the mole fraction from the same dots, with a stacked bar splitting in the ratio the counts demand - the point being that the denominator is n(A) + n(B), not n(A)

Screen 3 seals the vessel, lets both volatile components evaporate into the vapour space with the molecule mix following the two partial pressures, swings an analogue gauge up to the measured total, and then writes Raoult's law out and solves it line by line for p(B)deg in the student's own numbers, finishing with the back-substitution check

Screen 4 puts one mole of B in two chambers side by side: a liquid cube from M/rho and a vapour cube from RT/p(B)deg that visibly expands out of the liquid's size, both drawn at the true edge ratio - the cube root of the answer - and labelled as such instead of being distorted for drama
A suspense card then poses the division with the last value withheld, over a row of blanks, with a pulsing REVEAL ANSWER button

The reveal sprays the answer across the chamber in rough-edged graffiti lettering with drips and an offset shadow, sets off a burst of confetti and chemical glyphs, blinks the answer in the header, the gauge and the graffiti once and then stops, and unlocks the derivation

An interactive pressure-composition diagram drawn from the entered data, with both partial-pressure lines, the total, the measured level and the student's own solution marked - and a slider to explore any composition, reporting the two partial pressures, the total and the molality that would produce it

Two further diagram views, ratio against p(B)deg and ratio against temperature, showing the 1/p and linear-in-T dependence with the run's point on the curve - both kept locked until the answer has been revealed, because they plot the answer itself
A record of the run that fills in quantity by quantity, and a trial log of every completed run so two sets of data can be compared - with an insight card that names what can and cannot move the ratio
The headline cancellation is available as an experiment rather than a remark: change the mass of A, run again, and the gauges for n(A) and n(B) move while the answer does not
Six cards on the mistakes this question really produces, each re-running the model with one wrong assumption on the student's own numbers: 1600, 1523.81, 2.63, 2, 1882.35 and 5 x 10-4

Playback controls - pause, resume, replay, 0.5x / 1x / 2x - and a change-the-data button that returns to the rail with the entries kept; every box stays editable during the run and every instrument follows it
An optional sound toggle, off by default, that synthesises its bleeps in the browser so the page stays a single file with nothing fetched
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log, gated until the answer is revealed
Five concept cards that animate in when the answer lands and fill their numbers in only then, so the page cannot be read as a worked example before the experiment has been done
